COURSE REPORT Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2026-2027-SSCC-02-A At the July 14, 2026 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. for confirmation by the senate NEW COURSES CCJ302 : Research Methods & Design in Criminology & Criminal Justice, Fall 2027 (3 crs.) Overview of social science research in criminology and criminal justice, introducing methods, design, and data literacy.
Provides a criminological framework for designing, conducting, interpreting, and evaluating quantitative and qualitative research. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: CCJ major, C or better in CCJ101(H), and C or better in CCJ301; or by permission of instructor.
CCJ382 : Criminal Justice Myths & Realities, Fall 2027 (1 cr.) Overview of common myths and misperceptions about crime and criminal justice to analyze their origins, understand their real-world consequences, and evaluate evidence to separate fact from fiction. (Online/Lec.) CHS311 : Emergency Medical Technician, Spring 2027 (6 crs.) Provides students with the skills and knowledge to provide emergency care.

Successfully completing the course and passing the National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT) exam would prepare students to apply for licensure as an Emergency Medical Technician (EMT). (Lec. 4, Lab. 2) Pre: Permission of instructor.
PHY344 : Introductory Astrophysics II, Spring 2027 (3 crs.) Intermediate undergraduate course covering galaxies, their evolution, and Universe's structure, evolution, beginning, and ultimate fate. (Lec. 3) Pre: PHY306 SMC250 : Introduction to Sportscasting, Spring 2027 (3 crs.) Introduces students to various types of sportscasting with a heavy emphasis on writing and video package editing. (Lec. 3) Pre: SMC100; and SMC201 or SMC203.

COURSE MODIFICATIONS ART304 : Graphic Design II: Designing with Purpose, Spring 2027 Change title, credits (4 crs.) Approach project design situations faced by professional studio agencies in an educational context.
Current visual communication issues are solved through extensive research and the application of learned concepts and skills. (Studio 6) Pre: ART204.
May be repeated for up to 8 credits with permission of instructor, doing increasingly independent work.
AVS491 : Special Projects, Spring 2027 Change repeat criteria (1-12 crs.) Work that meets the individual needs of students in animal and veterinary science. (Independent Study) S/U grades only.
May be repeated for a total of 12 credits.
BAI305 : End-User Development for Business Analysis, Spring 2027 Change number and level (3 crs.) Introduction to developing software applications in the context of today's business environment.
Focus is on building a foundation for use of tools and techniques of business analytics.
Designed for students who have no prior experience in computer programming. (Lec. 3) Pre: Open to juniors and seniors in the College of Business Administration, completion of BAI310 or permission of instructor.

Not for graduate credit.
BAI455 : Business Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Applications, Spring 2027 Change prerequisite (3 crs.) Intermediate business applications of Business Analytics and Artificial Intelligence. (Lec. 3) Pre: BAI210, BAI356, and senior standing in a degree granting college; or by permission of instructor.
BAI456 : Database Management, Spring 2027 Change prerequisite (3 crs.) Modern concepts and methods in management of large volume of data; creation, design, and implementation of data models, integrity and security.
Use of database management systems (e.g.
RDBMS/NoSQL). (Lec. 3) Pre: Junior standing in a degree-granting college and BAI210 and BAI356; or CSC 201 or CSC 211.
Not for graduate credit.
BME484 : Biomedical Engineering Capstone Design I, Spring 2027 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Applications of engineering skills; team projects in biomedical areas such as neuroengineering, assistive technology, cardiopulmonary measurements, medical imaging, and modeling of physiological systems.
First of a two-course sequence. (Lec. 2, Lab. 3) Pre: BME207, BME360, and BME361, or by permission of instructor.

Not for graduate credit. (D1) CCJ101 : Introduction to Criminal Justice, Fall 2027 Change number and level (3 crs.) Formerly CCJ274(PSC274).
Introduces the U.S. criminal legal system, including understandings of and responses to crime, system components, and current challenges.
Examines the structure and function of police, courts, sentencing, and incarceration. (Lec. 3/Online)

CCJ301 : Criminological Theory, Fall 2027 Change number, title, add online modality (3 crs.) Formerly CCJ370.
Historical development of criminological theory; examination of the major theories of crime, criminality and delinquency; evaluation of competing theories. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: CCJ major, C or better in CCJ101 or CCJ101H, and sophomore standing; or by permission of instructor.
CMD460 : Speech and Language Disorders, Spring 2027 Remove online modality (3 crs.) Survey of developmental and acquired speech and language disorders.
Discussion includes etiology, symptomatology, and assessment. (Lec. 3) Pre: senior standing or permission of instructor.
Not for graduate credit.
EEC105 : Intro to Environmental Economics: Nature, Markets & Society, Fall 2027 Change title, description, add C3 outcome (3 crs.) Introduces environmental economics to link human decisions, nature, and policy.

Apply economic reasoning to address environmental challenges—from climate change to natural resource conservation—and discover innovative pathways toward sustainability. (Lec. 3/Online). (A2) (C3) GCH102G : Interdisciplinary Topics in Diversity and Inclusion, Spring 2027 New topic: Nutrition and the World Around Us (3-4 crs.) Study of important contemporary interdisciplinary topics with substantial relevance to diversity and inclusion, incorporating substantial attention to ethics. (Lec. 3-4) (C3) (GC) GWS400 : Critical Issues And Feminist Scholarship, Fall 2027 Change method of instruction, prerequisites, qualify for gen eds D1 and B2 (3 crs.) Theoretical and value questions in gender and women's studies; impact of feminist scholarship on traditional disciplines; feminist theory and research methods in selected fields; the future of feminism. (Lec. 3) Pre: GWS315, senior standing or permission of instructor. (B2) (D1) HDF497 : Special Problems, Spring 2027 Change description and prerequisites. (1-3 crs.) Advanced work primarily consisting of lab or field experiences.

Students must obtain written approval from proposed faculty supervisor prior to registration. (Independent Study) Pre: Sophomore standing and permission of instructor.
Not for graduate credit.
May be repeated for a maximum of 9 credits.
S/U only.
HLT491 : Experiential Learning Independent Study, Spring 2027 Change repeat criteria, editorial update to prereq (1-3 crs.) With faculty approval, students can select to complete an experiential learning independent study. (Independent Study) Pre: HLT300 and HLT450 and permission of director.
May be repeated for a maximum of 3 credits.
KIN470 : Biomechanics of Human Motion, Spring 2027 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Introduces advanced musculoskeletal biomechanics and the quantitative analysis of human movement.
Reviews the principles of motion and applies them to experimental and computational methods to evaluate human motion. (Lec. 3) Pre: PHY111 or PHY203; and BIO220, BIO222, and KIN370; and one of the following: MTH101, MTH103, MTH111, MTH131, or MTH141(H).
Open to Kinesiology and BME majors only, or by permission of instructor

NUT458 : Nutrition Education, Spring 2027 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Principles and practices of teaching individuals and groups to translate nutrition knowledge into action. Emphasis on research in and evaluation of nutrition education. (Lec. 3, Online) Pre: NUT395 or NUT396 or NUT440, or permission of instructor. (B2) (D1) PHY483 : Laboratory And Research Problems In Physics, Spring 2027 Change cross-listing (3 crs.) Cross-listed as (PHY) AST483. Research in current areas of physics. Students perform research projects with individual faculty members. Students in physics and physical oceanography may coordinate their research project with a faculty member of the Graduate School of Oceanography. (Lec. 1, Lab. 6) Pre: PHY381 and PHY382. SMC325 (JOR325) : Sports Writing, Spring 2027 Change subject code, description, add crosslisting, add for online instruction (3 crs.) Cross-listed as (SMC) JOR325. Focuses on basic sports writing skills as students cover local sports teams and learn to produce professional-quality journalism. (Lec. 2, Studio 1) Pre: SMC101, sophomore standing, and one of the following: JOR220, JOR320, JOR321, JOR341; or by permission of instructor. SOC375G (APG375G, GWS375G) : Global Perspectives on Reproduction, Fall 2027 Change number/level, method of instruction, prerequisites, add online modality (3 crs.) Cross-list with (SOC) APG375G, GWS375G. Examines the impact of inequalities of race, class, age, gender and sexuality on global variations in contraception, fertility, childbirth, and parenthood, and the ethical issues and social forces affecting reproduction. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: 6 credits in sociology, anthropology, gender and women's studies, or health studies; or permission of the instructor. (A2) (C2) (GC).

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION NOVEMBER 14, 2024 Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-03A At the October 31, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Informational Matters TEMPORARY COURSES COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: EEC 150X | Introduction to the Blue Economy, Effective Spring 2025 New Temporary Course (3 crs.) This course explores ocean-based economic activities, their role in the global economy, and tradeoffs. Students will learn tools to measure key tradeoffs and synergies, and explore strategies towards sustainable development. (Lec. 3) AVS 400X | Advanced Small Farm Management, Effective Spring 2025 Existing temporary course proposing a change to the prerequisites (4 crs.) Students integrate knowledge of husbandry with business/accounting principles, site -planning, assistance programs, and labor management of a small farm. Farm design, machinery skills, feed calculations, manure, and people management. (Lec. 3/Lab. 1) Pre: AVS 102, AVS 275; Completed or concurrent enrollment in AVS 304, AVS 332, AVS 212 or AVS 412, AVS 323 or AVS 324; senior standing or by permission of instructor. Not for graduate credit.

Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate COURSE CHANGES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: PLA 100 | Prior Learning Assessment Portfolio Development, Effective Spring 2025 Add URIO Version (1 cr.) Identification through self-assessment of student prior learning and appropriate methods for seeking credit.
Analysis and application of the process for developing a prior learning portfolio. (Seminar/Online/Accelerated Online Program) Pre: matriculated status and permission of the student's academic dean.
Offered through the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education.
S/U only.
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: MCE 301 | Application of Mechanics in Design, Effective Fall 2025 Change description (3 crs.) Concepts of engineering design, material selection, and failure theories.
Development of finite - element analysis for stress and deflection analysis.

Application to the design of mechanical components such as shafts, bolts, welded joints, and springs. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: CVE 220, credit or concurrent enrollment in ISE 240, and ((at least a 2.0 (C) average in PHY 203 (or 203H), MCE 262 (or 262H), CVE 220) and students must be admitted to the College of Engineering) or by permission of instructor.
MCE 302 | Design of Machinery, Effective Spring 2026 Change description (3 crs.) Comprehensive analysis and design of mechanisms and machine elements integrating multiple areas of mechanical engineering, including dynamics, fluid mechanics, and thermal sciences.
Application of multiphysics analysis to the design of machine components such as bearings, brakes, clutches, and power transmission elements. (Lec. 3) Pre: (MCE 201 or permission of instructor) and 263 and 301).
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: KIN 390 | Seminar in Kinesiology, Effective Spring 2025 Change prerequisites (2 crs.) Seminar for students preparing for careers and internships in Kinesiology.
Subject areas include career and internship opportunities, certification, and graduate school.
A variety of practicing professionals are featured speakers. (Seminar) Pre: 45 earned credits.

NUT 443 | Nutrition Assessment, Effective Spring 2029 Change prerequisites (4 crs.) Evaluation of nutritional status by dietary assessment, anthropometric measures, and nutrition - related health indicators.
Practice in body composition assessment, interpreting dietary and laboratory data, the Nutrition Care Process, documentation, and nutrition counseling. (Lec. 3, Lab. 2) Pre: NUT 210 and 395, and concurrent enrollment in NUT 444, or permission of instructor.

NUT 444 | Medical Nutrition Therapy I, Effective Fall 2028 Change prerequisites (3 crs.) Effects of disease on metabolism and nutritional requirements, implications for dietary change including Medical Nutrition Therapy, and factors affecting acceptance of such change. (Lec. 3).
Pre: credit or concurrent enrollment in NUT 441 and NUT 443.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: NRS 402 | Quantitative Ecology I, Effective Fall 2025 Change title (3 crs.) Overview of statistical design and analysis of ecological field measurements with an emphasis on probabilistic models used in wildlife population research and conservation.
Capstone. (Lec. 2, Lab. 3) Pre: BIO 262 or NRS 223, and STA 308 or 409, or permission of instructor.
Not for graduate credit.
NEW COURSES COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: EDC 323 | Infant and Toddler Education and Programming, Effective Summer 2024 (3 crs.) This course is designed to introduce students to the principles of infant and toddler programming.
Students will explore current research, theories, and practices in early childhood education, with a focus on the unique needs of infants and toddlers.

Students will learn about developmentally appropriate practice for infants and toddlers, strategies for guiding infant and toddler growth and development, the importance of responsive caregiving, infant/toddler mental health, and important elements of high-quality early learning environments for infants and toddlers. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: Admission to the College of Education or the Early Childhood Education Program, or by permission of instructor.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: HLT 350 | Special Topics in Public Health, Effective Spring 2025 (3 crs.) This course will cover special topics in public health, such as public health research and methods, public health concerns, and public health approaches to promoting health and well-being. (Lec. 3) Pre: HLT 300 with a C or higher, or by permission of instructor for students of at least junior standing.
KIN 222 | Medical Terminology, Effective Summer 2025 (2 crs.) Framework for medical terminology used by health care professionals.
Analyze medical terms, learn word roots and origins, spelling, definitions, and pronunciations.

Major pathological conditions, common disorders, and prescribed medications. (Online) NUT 446 | Nutrition and Disease, Effective Spring 2026 (3 crs.) An introductory course in Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) for pharmacy majors to gain a basic understanding of MNT in various disease states and how metabolism is affected by drug-nutrient interactions. (Lec. 3).
Pre: Enrolled in PharmD program, or by permission of instructor.
Not for graduate credit.

PSY 260 | Psyched About Culture: Intro to Cross-Cultural Psychology, Effective Spring 2025 (3 crs.) This course examines how culture shapes people’s psychological processes. It focuses on the ways cultural background influences perception, emotions, relationships, health, and behaviors. Using a cross - cultural approach, the emphasis is on looking at culture as a framework for understanding people's thoughts and behaviors across the globe. (Lec. 3/Online) Pre: PSY 113; PSY BS major or permission of instructor.

NEW PROGRAM REPORT curriculum & standards committee Report 2025-2026-casc-08-c At the April 23, 2026 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. for confirmation by the senate NEW PROGRAM Interdisciplinary & Applied Artificial Intelligence - BS, Spring 2026 Appendix A The Interdisciplinary & Applied Artificial Intelligence (AI) program prepares students to apply AI technologies to complex, interdisciplinary real-world challenges. The program is grounded in technical foundations and interdisciplinary collaboration. Students develop hands-on skills in data management, analytics programming, machine learning, visualization, and generative AI tools. They also examine the broader implications of AI for organizations. Emphasis is placed on fairness and responsible AI use. Through project-based coursework, innovation and entrepreneurship experiences, and an applied internship, students learn to work in cross-functional teams and translate AI insights into actionable solutions. Graduates of the program are prepared for roles that require technical fluency and critical thinking, including positions in analytics, innovation, and emerging AI-enabled fields, as well as for graduate study. Major Requirements: BAI110 or EGR101 and EGR106 BAI212 or CSC201 or CSC200 or EGR241 CSC161(DSP161) DSP181G(BIO181G) or EGR316G(PHL316G) BAI310 or ISE325 BAI356 BAI454 BAI457 or BAI405 or CSC310(DSP310) BAI476 or EGR441 INE349 (2 times with 2 different approved topics) EGR404 or INE349 with an approved topic

BAI456 BUS392(IAI392) or ITR302 BAI111 or MTH131 or MTH141or MTH141H BAI210 or STA308 or STA409 or ISE311 WRT290 Professional Electives: Please select two courses from the following: BAI455 MKT467 SCA467 FIN412 FIN431 FIN433 GEO404(OCG404, NRS404) GEO422(NRS422, MAF422) CMB320 CSC521 EGR444 or other approved courses Students must complete a minimum of 55 credits in the major. Free Electives: Two. Students can choose General Education courses and free electives to make up the balance of 120 credits, up to 65 credits. Students must have a minimum GPA of 2.5 to move into the major. A minimum overall GPA of 2.0 and a minimum of 2.0 is required from the major requirements for graduation. A minimum of 120 credits is required for graduation. At least 42 credits must be at the 300-level or above.

The primary goal of the BS in Interdisciplinary Applied Artificial Intelligence is to prepare graduates who can apply artificial intelligence responsibly, creatively, and effectively across domains, integrating technical skills with ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and real-world problem solving.
The program emphasizes applied and lifelong learning, workforce relevance, and societal impact, ensuring that graduates are prepared for both immediate employment and long- term career adaptability.
It advances student success, retention, timely degree completion, and career readiness.
The program’s applied focus, interdisciplinary design, and integration of experiential learning opportunities support students in developing market- relevant skills that align with workforce needs.
By embedding internships, project-based learning, and applied AI coursework throughout the curriculum, the program enhances students’ engagement, persistence, and post-graduation outcomes while positioning URI graduates to succeed in a rapidly evolving, AI-enabled economy.

The vision is to provide students with deep knowledge of AI systems and expertise in transferring and applying AI to a variety of problem types.
This program will cover knowledge of the AI ecosystem including the ability to work in interdisciplinary teams with data and domain experts to collect, clean organize, and sample data, match the problem and data to the right intelligent computational tool (there are many types of AI, each with its strengths and weaknesses), tailor, build on top of, and adapt these tools to the problems at hand, support the safe, secure, ethical and accurate reporting of the results to domain experts, and guide teams in deciding if the analytical results make sense.
Students will learn how to use, tailor and augment AI so that the AI can serve as assistants in problem solving, with the human as the master, well versed in the interpretation, and ethical and societal implications of the use of the powerful AI that they will wield.
All of this is in the context of a world in which educators and potential employers are concerned with the lack of digital skills among today’s students and graduates.

To be well educated and prepared for the modern workplace, students must learn to acquire applied technology skills and also to transfer these technologies to specific problems as they arise.
Thus this program is not intended to train students to develop new AI, but to become experts in mastering, adapting, building upon, and deploying existing and evolving intelligent computational artifacts.
We will help students to master the AI tools of today but also help them to understand that these are only contemporary examples to sharpen their problem solving, and learning skills, and give them a leg up as they enter the workplace.
As the world changes and embraces new technologies such as digital twins, and quantum computing, both already inextricably intertwined with AI, we propose a major that is flexible enough that it can evolve with emerging intelligent technologies.
The program advances the University’s goals by preparing students to address complex real-world challenges through the responsible and creative application of emerging technologies.

The curriculum integrates applied coursework, project-based learning, and internships, ensuring that students develop both technical expertise and transferable skills that support career readiness and lifelong learning.
The program reflects the University’s commitment to interdisciplinary problem-solving and collaboration across colleges and departments.
The program also contributes to the University’s role in supporting economic development, innovation, and the future of work in Rhode Island and beyond.

COURSE REPORT Special Summer Curriculum Committee Report 2026-2027-SSCC-01-A At the July 14, 2026 meeting of the Special Summer Curriculum Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for approval. informational matters TEMPORARY COURSE BPS346X: Self-Paced Skills Laboratory for Pharmaceutical Scientists, Fall 2026 (2 crs.) Explores core experimental techniques used in biomedical and pharmaceutical research.
Supports students before or during independent research, and emphasizes practical skill development, quantitative reasoning, and the connection between experimental data and biological or pharmacological questions.
Students will learn how to design assays, generate and analyze data, and evaluate experimental results with an emphasis on accuracy, reproducibility, and good laboratory practice.
Students will select specialized experimental modules aligned with their research interests or future laboratory placements.

By the end of the course, students will work more independently and effectively in biomedical or pharmaceutical research laboratories, with a strong foundation in experimental technique, data analysis, and scientific communication. (Lab. 3) Pre: BPS345 and permission by the chair of BPS. for confirmation by the senate NEW COURSES BPS493: Scholars in Biomedical & Pharmaceutical Sciences, Fall 2026 (1 cr.) Student forum to present research projects, discuss experimental design and results, and engage in scientific dialogue with peers and faculty.
Research topics may span areas such as drug discovery, pharmacology, toxicology, pharmaceutics, pharmacokinetics, environmental health, and natural products.
Through structured presentations and discussion, students develop skills in scientific communication, data interpretation, and critical evaluation of research.
Exposes participants to diverse research approaches within pharmaceutical sciences, helping students connect laboratory research with concepts

learned in the classroom.
Students will strengthen their ability to present scientific work professionally, ask thoughtful questions, and engage in scholarly discussion—skills essential for graduate study, professional programs, and careers in biomedical research.
